subject: Physics
title: Current Electricity
summary: Current Electricity explains how charge flows through a conductor: what current and current density are, why Ohm's law works (the drift of electrons and relaxation time), how resistivity depends on material and temperature, how a cell drives current through its own internal resistance, and how Kirchhoff's rules and the Wheatstone bridge solve any circuit. It is the second half of Unit II (Current Electricity) and gives the board paper at least one derivation and one circuit numerical every year.

exam_profile.weightage: Units I and II (Electrostatics and Current Electricity, Chapters 1 to 3) together carry 16 marks in the CBSE Class 12 Physics paper. This chapter typically contributes about 6 to 8 marks: usually one 3-mark derivation or numerical (drift velocity, cells in parallel, Kirchhoff's rules or the Wheatstone bridge), one or two 1-mark questions, and often a part of a case-based or 5-mark question.

question_types.note: Resistance of a stretched or cut wire; which bulb glows brighter in series; how drift velocity changes with length or area; unit of mobility or conductivity; terminal voltage of a cell; equivalent emf of cells in parallel; the balance condition of a Wheatstone bridge; V–I graphs at two temperatures.

Why resistivity of a semiconductor falls with temperature; why manganin is used for standard resistances; why a bulb lights instantly though drift speed is tiny; Kirchhoff's rules and conservation laws; terminal voltage exceeding emf while charging.

Define drift velocity, mobility, emf or internal resistance; ratio of drift speeds of two wires in series or parallel; V–I graph of a non-ohmic device; graphs of terminal voltage against R or I; why alloys are used for heaters and standard resistances; a two-line numerical on V = ε − Ir.

Derive I = neAv<sub>d</sub> and ρ = m/(ne<sup>2</sup>τ); derive the equivalent emf and internal resistance of two cells in parallel; apply Kirchhoff's rules to a two-loop circuit; derive the Wheatstone bridge balance condition; power in series and parallel combinations of heaters or bulbs.

Full drift-velocity treatment with the temperature dependence of resistivity; Kirchhoff's rules with the Wheatstone bridge derivation and a numerical; emf, internal resistance and terminal voltage with the V–R and V–I graphs and a numerical on finding ε and r from two readings.
A passage on the temperature dependence of resistivity, on drift velocity and mobility, or on a cell with internal resistance, followed by four short parts, one of them a one-step numerical.

Kirchhoff's rules and their use in two-loop circuits with two cells
Wheatstone bridge: balance condition derived from Kirchhoff's rules
Cells in parallel: equivalent emf and internal resistance; cells in series
Emf, internal resistance and terminal voltage; V–R and V–I graphs; finding ε and r from two readings

Electrical power: bulbs and heaters in series and parallel; why power is transmitted at high voltage

sections.heading: 3.1 Introduction
sections.body:
Chapters 1 and 2 dealt with charges at rest. This chapter is about charges in motion, that is, electric current, and it stays within steady currents: currents that do not change with time. Almost everything you use, from a torch to a lift motor, runs on current, so the chapter sits close to daily life, and the board treats it as a chapter of definitions, one central derivation and circuit problems.

The story runs in a fixed order. First we define current and see what carries it in a metal. Then Ohm's law is stated as an experimental fact and explained by the drift of free electrons, which is the derivation examiners ask for most. From that model we get resistivity, its dependence on temperature, and the materials used for heaters and standard resistances. Then energy and power. Then the source that keeps a current going, the cell, with its emf and internal resistance, and combinations of cells. Finally two general tools, Kirchhoff's rules and the Wheatstone bridge, that let you solve circuits that are not simple series or parallel networks.

Two things were removed in the rationalised syllabus and are not examined now: the meter bridge and the potentiometer, and the colour code of carbon resistors. Series and parallel combinations of resistors are assumed from Class 10 and still get used inside problems.
sections.tip: Read the chapter as one chain: current → drift velocity → Ohm's law → resistivity → power → cells → Kirchhoff → Wheatstone. Every board question sits on one link of this chain.

sections.heading: 3.2 Electric Current
sections.body:
Electric current through an area is the rate of flow of charge across that area. If a net charge q flows across the area in time t, the average current is I = q/t; if the flow varies, the instantaneous current is I = dq/dt, the limit of ΔQ/Δt as Δt → 0. The SI unit is the ampere (A): 1 A = 1 C s−1. Currents in a household wire are of the order of an ampere, in a nerve a microampere, and in lightning tens of thousands of amperes.

By convention the direction of current is the direction in which positive charge would move, so in a metal wire the current points opposite to the motion of the electrons that actually carry it. Note two facts the examiner likes. Current is a scalar, even though it has a direction in a wire: currents add by ordinary algebra at a junction, not by the parallelogram law. And the same current flows at every cross-section of a series circuit, because charge does not pile up anywhere in a steady state.

Along with current, this chapter uses current density j, the current per unit area through a surface held normal to the flow: j = I/A, unit A m−2. Unlike current, j is a vector, pointing along the direction of flow of positive charge. If the normal to the area makes an angle θ with the direction of flow, I = jA cos θ. Current density is what links the microscopic picture (electrons drifting) to the macroscopic one (current in a wire), and it appears in the vector form of Ohm's law in section 3.4.

where: current density (A m<sup>−2</sup>), a vector along the flow of positive charge

sections.tip: If a question asks 'is current a vector?', the answer is no: it does not obey vector addition. Current density is the vector.

sections.heading: 3.3 Electric Currents in Conductors
sections.body:
A charge placed in an electric field moves, so a current needs both mobile charges and a field. In a solid metal the positive ions are locked into a lattice and only the outermost electrons, the free or conduction electrons, can move. In an electrolyte both positive and negative ions move. In an insulator there are almost no free carriers, so even a strong field gives a negligible current.

With no field applied, the free electrons in a metal move randomly with thermal speeds of about 105 m s−1, colliding with the ions. The velocities point in all directions, so at any instant as many electrons cross a plane one way as the other and the net current is zero. Now imagine a cylinder of the metal with a thin layer of positive charge on one end face and negative charge on the other: there is a field inside, electrons are pushed towards the positive face, and a current flows. But as they arrive they neutralise the charge, the field dies away and the current stops in a very short time. To keep a steady current we need something that keeps replenishing the charges on the two ends, and that is what a cell or battery does: it maintains a steady potential difference between the ends of the conductor.

So the picture for the rest of the chapter is: a source maintains a constant field inside the conductor; the free electrons acquire a small steady average velocity opposite to the field on top of their random motion; and that average velocity, the drift velocity, is what constitutes the current. In a steady current the electron gas as a whole does not accelerate indefinitely because collisions with the ions keep resetting its velocity, which is exactly the origin of resistance treated in section 3.5.
sections.tip: The electrons in a metal are 'free' only to move within the metal; they do not leave it. Do not write that electrons flow out of the wire into the battery and vanish; the circuit is a closed loop.

sections.heading: 3.4 Ohm's Law
sections.body:
Ohm's law (1827) is an experimental statement: at constant temperature and other physical conditions, the current through a conductor is directly proportional to the potential difference across its ends, V ∝ I, or V = IR. The constant R is the resistance of the conductor, unit ohm (Ω): 1 Ω = 1 V A−1. Resistance depends on the material, the dimensions and the temperature of the conductor, not on V or I.

How R depends on dimensions can be argued directly. Put two identical slabs of length l in series: the same current flows through a slab of length 2l with twice the potential difference, so R ∝ l. Put them side by side: the same V drives twice the current through an area 2A, so R ∝ 1/A. Hence R = ρl/A, where ρ is the resistivity, a property of the material alone, unit Ω m. Its reciprocal σ = 1/ρ is the conductivity, unit S m−1 (Ω−1 m−1). The reciprocal of resistance, G = 1/R, is the conductance, unit siemens (S).

The board also expects the vector form of Ohm's law, which links the field inside the conductor to the current density. Take a conductor of length l and area A carrying current I with a uniform field E along it. Then V = El and I = jA. Substituting in V = IR = I ρl/A gives El = jρl, so E = ρj, or equivalently j = σE. This form has no reference to the shape of the conductor and is the statement we will reproduce from the electron model in the next section.

A conductor obeying Ohm's law is called ohmic, and its V–I graph is a straight line through the origin whose slope (V against I) is R. Ohm's law is not a fundamental law of nature; it is a property of many materials over a range of conditions, and section 3.6 lists where it fails.

where: electric field inside the conductor (V m<sup>−1</sup>)

sections.tip: When a wire is stretched, its volume is constant, so doubling the length halves the area and the resistance becomes 4 times. In general R ∝ l<sup>2</sup> for a stretched wire of fixed volume.

sections.heading: 3.5 Drift of Electrons and the Origin of Resistivity
sections.body:
This is the derivation the board asks for most from this chapter. Write it in these steps.

Step 1, drift velocity. Consider a metal with n free electrons per unit volume, each of mass m and charge −e, in a field E. Each electron feels a force −eE and an acceleration a = −eE/m. Between two collisions with the ions an electron accelerates; at each collision its velocity is reset to a random thermal value. If the average time between successive collisions is τ, the relaxation time, then at any instant the velocities of the electrons since their last collision have been increased on average by aτ. The random thermal velocities average to zero, so the average velocity of the electrons, the drift velocity, is vd = −eEτ/m. It is opposite to E and, unlike a free acceleration, it is constant.

Step 2, current in terms of drift velocity. In a wire of cross-section A, the electrons that cross a given section in time Δt are those within a length vdΔt of it: number = n A vd Δt, charge = neAvdΔt. Hence I = neAvd, and the current density j = I/A = nevd.

Step 3, Ohm's law and resistivity. Substituting vd = eEτ/m in magnitude: j = (ne2τ/m)E. Comparing with j = σE gives σ = ne2τ/m, so ρ = m/(ne2τ). Since n and τ do not depend on E, ρ is constant and V = IR follows, which is Ohm's law.

Put in numbers for copper (Example 3.1): a 1.5 A current in a wire of area 10−7 m2 gives vd ≈ 1 mm s−1, far smaller than the thermal speed (~105 m s−1) and utterly unlike the speed at which the field itself is set up along the wire (close to the speed of light). That is why a bulb lights the instant a switch is closed: electrons everywhere in the circuit start drifting at once.

3.5.1 Mobility. The mobility μ of a charge carrier is the magnitude of its drift velocity per unit electric field, μ = |vd|/E = eτ/m. Its SI unit is m2 V−1 s−1. In terms of mobility, σ = neμ; for a material with more than one kind of carrier (a semiconductor, an electrolyte) the conductivities of the carriers add.

formulas.expr: v<sub>d</sub> = eEτ/m (magnitude); direction opposite to E for electrons
where: relaxation time, average time between collisions (~10<sup>−14</sup> s in metals)
electron mass 9.1 × 10<sup>−31</sup> kg and charge 1.6 × 10<sup>−19</sup> C
number density of free electrons (m<sup>−3</sup>), ~8.5 × 10<sup>28</sup> for copper

sections.tip: In ratio questions remember: wires in series carry the same I, so v<sub>d</sub> ∝ 1/A; wires in parallel have the same V, so for equal lengths v<sub>d</sub> is the same regardless of thickness (E = V/l is the same). Drift velocity depends on E, not directly on I.

sections.heading: 3.6 Limitations of Ohm's Law
sections.body:
Ohm's law holds for metals and many alloys over a wide range of conditions, but it is not universal. NCERT lists three ways in which a material or device can deviate, and each has a characteristic V–I graph that you should be able to sketch.

(a) V stops being proportional to I. For a metallic wire that heats up as the current increases, the resistance rises, and the V–I line bends upwards at large currents (more V for the same increase in I). The graph is a straight line at small currents and curves away from it later.

(b) The relation depends on the sign of V. For a p–n junction diode, reversing the polarity of V does not reverse the current with the same magnitude: a small forward voltage gives a large current, while the same reverse voltage gives almost none. The V–I graph is not symmetric about the origin.

(c) The relation is not unique. For some materials, such as gallium arsenide (GaAs), there is a region where increasing V actually decreases I (negative resistance), so more than one value of V gives the same current. The graph rises, reaches a peak and then falls before rising again.

Devices that do not obey Ohm's law are called non-ohmic, and they are the basis of electronics (Chapter 14). Remember that even for a non-ohmic device the ratio V/I at any point can still be called its resistance at that operating point; what fails is the constancy of that ratio. When the examiner asks 'state the conditions under which Ohm's law is valid', the expected words are: constant temperature and unchanged physical conditions (mechanical strain, pressure) of the conductor.
sections.tip: Draw the diode V–I graph with a steep forward branch in the first quadrant and a nearly flat reverse branch in the third; the GaAs graph must show a clear peak followed by a dip. A symmetric straight line through the origin earns zero for a non-ohmic device.

sections.heading: 3.7 Resistivity of Various Materials
sections.body:
Resistivity spans about 24 orders of magnitude, and materials are grouped by it. Conductors (metals) have ρ between about 10−8 and 10−6 Ω m: silver is the best at 1.6 × 10−8 Ω m, then copper 1.7 × 10−8, aluminium 2.7 × 10−8. Insulators have ρ of the order of 1010 to 1016 Ω m (glass, hard rubber, fused quartz at the top of that range). Semiconductors such as germanium and silicon lie in between, and their resistivity is very sensitive to temperature and to tiny amounts of impurities, which is what makes them useful in electronics.

Two families of alloys matter for exam questions. Nichrome (ρ ≈ 1.0 × 10−6 Ω m, about 60 times copper) has high resistivity, a high melting point and does not oxidise easily at red heat, so it is used for the heating elements of heaters, toasters and irons. Manganin and constantan have high resistivity and, more importantly, an almost zero temperature coefficient of resistivity, so their resistance stays fixed as they warm up in use; they are used for standard resistances, resistance boxes and wire-wound resistors.

Commercial resistors are of two kinds: wire-wound resistors made from alloys like manganin for values up to about 100 kΩ, and carbon resistors, which are cheap, compact and used in electronic circuits for higher values. The colour-code convention for reading a carbon resistor's value was part of the older syllabus and is no longer examined.

A short-answer question here usually asks why a particular alloy is chosen: link the property to the use. Heating element needs high ρ (large heat per unit length for a manageable length) and stability at high temperature. Standard resistance needs a value that does not drift, so low α, and a resistivity high enough that the coil is not impractically long.

formulas.expr: ρ<sub>conductors</sub> ~ 10<sup>−8</sup>–10<sup>−6</sup> Ω m; ρ<sub>insulators</sub> ~ 10<sup>10</sup>–10<sup>16</sup> Ω m
where: resistivity (Ω m); semiconductors lie between the two ranges

sections.tip: Silver is a better conductor than copper. Copper is used for wiring because it is far cheaper, not because it conducts better.

sections.heading: 3.8 Temperature Dependence of Resistivity
sections.body:
Over a limited range of temperatures not too far from room temperature, the resistivity of a metal rises linearly with temperature: ρT = ρ0[1 + α(T − T0)], where ρ0 is the resistivity at a reference temperature T0 and α is the temperature coefficient of resistivity, unit °C−1 or K−1. Since R ∝ ρ for a given conductor, the same relation holds for resistance: RT = R0[1 + α(T − T0)]. This is the formula behind every 'find the steady temperature of the heating element' numerical: find R at the two temperatures from V/I, then solve for T.

The model of section 3.5 explains the trend. ρ = m/(ne2τ), so ρ depends on the carrier density n and the relaxation time τ. In a metal, n is fixed by the material and does not change with temperature, but as T rises the ions vibrate more, collisions become more frequent, τ falls and ρ rises: α is positive (copper α ≈ 3.9 × 10−3 °C−1). The ρ–T graph for copper is nearly a straight line rising with T, curving slightly at low temperatures. For alloys such as nichrome and manganin, ρ is high and nearly independent of temperature, so the graph is almost flat (manganin α ≈ 0.002 × 10−3 °C−1). For semiconductors and insulators, heating frees many more carriers, so n increases with T much faster than τ falls, and ρ decreases with temperature: α is negative. The ρ–T graph of a semiconductor falls steeply as T rises.

A worked pattern (Example 3.4): a platinum resistance thermometer has R = 5 Ω at the ice point, 5.23 Ω at the steam point and 5.795 Ω in a bath, so the bath temperature is t = (Rt − R0)/(R100 − R0) × 100 = (0.795/0.23) × 100 = 345.65 °C. The board also asks the reverse: given α, R0 at 27 °C and the steady current from a 230 V supply, find the working temperature. Set up RT = V/I, then T − T0 = (RT − R0)/(R0α).

formulas.expr: ρ<sub>T</sub> = ρ<sub>0</sub>[1 + α(T − T<sub>0</sub>)]; R<sub>T</sub> = R<sub>0</sub>[1 + α(T − T<sub>0</sub>)]
where: temperature coefficient of resistivity (°C<sup>−1</sup>); positive for metals, ~0 for manganin, negative for semiconductors
reference temperature, usually 0 °C or room temperature
resistance at T<sub>0</sub> and at T

sections.tip: When you explain the temperature dependence, always quote ρ = m/(ne<sup>2</sup>τ) and say which factor dominates: τ for metals (falls), n for semiconductors (rises). That one sentence is the marking point.

sections.heading: 3.9 Electrical Energy, Power
sections.body:
Consider a conductor with a potential difference V between its ends A and B (V = VA − VB > 0) carrying current I from A to B. In time Δt a charge ΔQ = IΔt moves from A to B, and its potential energy falls by ΔUpot = ΔQ(VB − VA) = −IVΔt. By energy conservation the charges should gain kinetic energy equal to this, but in a conductor they collide with the ions and hand the energy over to the lattice as heat. So the energy dissipated in the conductor in time Δt is ΔW = IVΔt, and the power dissipated is P = IV. With Ohm's law this becomes P = I2R = V2/R. This is the Joule heating that runs heaters, bulbs and fuses. The source (a cell, a generator) supplies this power by doing work on the charges.

Which form to use depends on what is held fixed. In a series connection the current is common, so P = I2R and the larger resistance dissipates more. In a parallel connection the voltage is common, so P = V2/R and the smaller resistance dissipates more. That is why a 60 W bulb glows brighter than a 100 W bulb when the two (both rated 220 V) are put in series: the 60 W bulb has the larger resistance (R = V2/P = 807 Ω against 484 Ω) and the same current passes through both.

The other standard question is power transmission. A power station delivers power P at voltage V to a load through cables of total resistance Rc. The current in the cables is I = P/V, so the power wasted as heat in the cables is Pc = I2Rc = P2Rc/V2. For a fixed power to be delivered, the loss falls as 1/V2, so transmission is done at very high voltages (hundreds of kilovolts) and stepped down by transformers near the consumer (Chapter 7). Thick low-resistance cables help too, but the voltage is the decisive factor.

formulas.expr: P = VI = I<sup>2</sup>R = V<sup>2</sup>/R; energy W = VIt
where: energy in time t (J); 1 kWh = 3.6 × 10<sup>6</sup> J
power lost in transmission cables of resistance R<sub>c</sub> when power P is sent at voltage V

sections.tip: The wattage printed on a bulb is its power at the rated voltage. In a series combination the bulbs are not at rated voltage, so first find each resistance from R = V<sup>2</sup>/P and then use P = I<sup>2</sup>R with the common current.

sections.heading: 3.10 Cells, emf, Internal Resistance
sections.body:
A cell has two electrodes, positive (P) and negative (N), dipped in an electrolyte. Chemical action at the electrodes maintains a potential difference between them even when nothing is connected. The emf ε of the cell is the potential difference between its terminals when no current is drawn from it (open circuit); equivalently, it is the work done by the cell per unit charge in carrying positive charge from the negative to the positive terminal inside the cell. Despite the name, emf is a potential difference, not a force, and its unit is the volt.

The electrolyte itself opposes the flow of charge; this is the internal resistance r of the cell. It depends on the nature and concentration of the electrolyte, the area of the electrodes, their separation and the temperature; it is small for a car battery and large for a dry cell.

Connect an external resistance R across the cell. The current is I = ε/(R + r), and the potential difference across the terminals, the terminal voltage, is V = IR = ε − Ir. So V is less than ε whenever the cell delivers current; the two are equal only when I = 0 (open circuit, or r = 0). The maximum current the cell can give is ε/r, when R = 0 (short circuit). If the cell is being charged, current is driven into it through the positive terminal and the terminal voltage exceeds the emf: V = ε + Ir.

Two graphs are examined. Terminal voltage against current I is a straight line with intercept ε on the V-axis and slope −r, so a V–I plot of a cell gives both ε and r. Terminal voltage against external resistance R rises from 0 at R = 0 and approaches ε as R becomes large. From two readings of I with known R1 and R2 you solve ε = I1(R1 + r) = I2(R2 + r) for r and ε. Another useful rearrangement: r = (ε/V − 1)R.

formulas.expr: I = ε/(R + r); V = ε − Ir = IR
where: terminal voltage (V), less than ε while discharging

sections.tip: Emf and terminal voltage are both measured in volts, so 'unit' does not distinguish them. The distinction is: emf is for open circuit (I = 0); terminal voltage is what a voltmeter across the cell reads while current flows.

sections.heading: 3.11 Cells in Series and in Parallel
sections.body:
Series. Let cell 1 (ε1, r1) and cell 2 (ε2, r2) be joined with the negative terminal of the first to the positive of the second, carrying the same current I. Across the first, VAB = ε1 − Ir1; across the second, VBC = ε2 − Ir2. Adding, VAC = (ε1 + ε2) − I(r1 + r2). Comparing with V = εeq − Ireq: εeq = ε1 + ε2 and req = r1 + r2. If the second cell is connected the other way round (negative to negative), εeq = ε1 − ε2 with the same req. For n identical cells in series, εeq = nε, req = nr.

Parallel (the derivation the board asks for). Now connect the two positive terminals at B1 and the two negatives at B2, and let the cells supply currents I1 and I2 to the external circuit, so I = I1 + I2. Both cells have the same terminal voltage V across them: V = ε1 − I1r1 and V = ε2 − I2r2. Hence I1 = (ε1 − V)/r1, I2 = (ε2 − V)/r2, and

I = (ε1/r1 + ε2/r2) − V(1/r1 + 1/r2).

Solving for V: V = (ε1r2 + ε2r1)/(r1 + r2) − I r1r2/(r1 + r2). Comparing with V = εeq − Ireq:

εeq = (ε1r2 + ε2r1)/(r1 + r2), req = r1r2/(r1 + r2), i.e. 1/req = 1/r1 + 1/r2.

A neat form to remember: εeq/req = ε1/r1 + ε2/r2. If one cell is reversed, replace ε2 by −ε2. For n identical cells in parallel, εeq = ε and req = r/n: parallel cells do not increase the voltage, they lower the internal resistance and can supply a larger current. A 1.5 V cell (r = 0.2 Ω) and a 2.0 V cell (r = 0.3 Ω) in parallel give εeq = (1.5 × 0.3 + 2.0 × 0.2)/0.5 = 0.85/0.5 = 1.7 V and req = 0.06/0.5 = 0.12 Ω.

formulas.expr: Series: ε<sub>eq</sub> = ε<sub>1</sub> + ε<sub>2</sub>, r<sub>eq</sub> = r<sub>1</sub> + r<sub>2</sub>
where: use ε<sub>1</sub> − ε<sub>2</sub> if the cells oppose
= ε<sub>1</sub>/r<sub>1</sub> + ε<sub>2</sub>/r<sub>2</sub>, the form that extends to n cells

sections.tip: The parallel formula is a weighted average of the emfs, weighted by the other cell's resistance. Sanity-check every answer: ε<sub>eq</sub> must lie between ε<sub>1</sub> and ε<sub>2</sub>, and r<sub>eq</sub> must be smaller than both r<sub>1</sub> and r<sub>2</sub>.

sections.heading: 3.12 Kirchhoff's Rules
sections.body:
Series and parallel formulas cannot handle every circuit, for instance one with two cells in different branches. Kirchhoff's two rules (1845) can. First label every branch with a current and an assumed direction; if the answer comes out negative, the current actually flows the other way.

Junction rule (first rule). At any junction the sum of the currents entering equals the sum of the currents leaving. It follows from conservation of charge: in a steady current, charge cannot accumulate at a junction, so what flows in must flow out.

Loop rule (second rule). The algebraic sum of the changes in potential around any closed loop of the circuit is zero. It follows from the fact that electric potential is single-valued: going round a loop and returning to the starting point must bring you back to the same potential. It is equivalent to conservation of energy in the circuit.

Sign conventions (state them in the answer). Going round the loop in the chosen direction: crossing a resistor in the direction of the current is a drop, −IR; against the current it is a rise, +IR. Crossing a cell from its negative to its positive terminal is a rise, +ε; from positive to negative, −ε. The internal resistance of a cell is treated as an ordinary resistor in series with it.

Method for a numerical. (1) Mark currents so that the junction rule is used as early as possible (for two branches joining a third, call the third I1 + I2). (2) Write the loop rule for as many independent loops as there are unknowns. (3) Solve. For example, take a 12 V cell (2 Ω) and a 6 V cell (1 Ω) in two parallel branches feeding a 4 Ω resistor. With I1, I2 from the two cells and I1 + I2 through 4 Ω: 12 − 2I1 − 4(I1 + I2) = 0 and 6 − I2 − 4(I1 + I2) = 0, giving I1 = 18/7 A, I2 = −6/7 A: the 6 V cell is being charged by the 12 V cell. NCERT Example 3.5 uses the same rules with symmetry to find the resistance of a cube of twelve 1 Ω edges across a body diagonal: 5/6 Ω.

where: currents at a junction; based on conservation of charge

formulas.expr: Loop rule: ∑ε − ∑IR = 0 around any closed loop
where: +ε from − to + terminal; −IR along the current

sections.tip: Use exactly as many loop equations as unknown currents, and never take a loop that is just the sum of two loops already used. Keep the sign convention fixed for the whole answer; changing it halfway is the commonest source of a wrong sign.

sections.heading: 3.13 Wheatstone Bridge
sections.body:
The Wheatstone bridge is the standard application of Kirchhoff's rules and the usual 3-mark derivation. Four resistors R1, R2, R3, R4 form a quadrilateral ABCD, with R1 in arm AB, R2 in arm BC, R3 in arm AD and R4 in arm DC. A cell is connected between A and C, and a galvanometer of resistance G between B and D. The bridge is balanced when the galvanometer shows no deflection, Ig = 0, which happens when B and D are at the same potential.

Derivation. Let the cell send current I into A, splitting into I1 through R1 and I2 through R3. At balance Ig = 0, so by the junction rule at B the current I1 continues through R2, and at D the current I2 continues through R4.

Loop rule for loop ADBA: −I2R3 + 0·G + I1R1 = 0, so I1R1 = I2R3.

Loop rule for loop CBDC: I2R4 + 0·G − I1R2 = 0, so I1R2 = I2R4.

Dividing the second by the first: R2/R1 = R4/R3. This is the balance condition. Written as P/Q = R/S it says the ratio of the resistances in the two arms meeting at B equals the ratio in the two arms meeting at D; the galvanometer resistance and the cell's emf and internal resistance drop out of it, which is the whole point.

Use. Take R4 as the unknown, R3 a known standard, and adjust R2 (with R1 fixed) until the galvanometer reads zero; then R4 = R2R3/R1. The measurement is a null method, so it does not depend on the calibration of the galvanometer, and it is most sensitive when the four resistances are of the same order. Two facts often asked: interchanging the cell and the galvanometer does not disturb the balance (the condition is symmetric), and at balance the galvanometer and cell branch can be removed or short-circuited without changing the currents in the arms. When the bridge is not balanced, you must go back to Kirchhoff's rules for all three loops, as in NCERT Example 3.7.

formulas.expr: Balance: R<sub>2</sub>/R<sub>1</sub> = R<sub>4</sub>/R<sub>3</sub>, i.e. P/Q = R/S; unknown R<sub>4</sub> = R<sub>2</sub>R<sub>3</sub>/R<sub>1</sub>
where: galvanometer current, zero at balance (V<sub>B</sub> = V<sub>D</sub>)

key_terms.definition: The rate of flow of electric charge through a cross-section of a conductor, I = dq/dt. SI unit ampere; a scalar whose conventional direction is that of positive charge.
Current per unit area through a surface normal to the flow, j = I/A, unit A m<sup>−2</sup>. A vector along the flow of positive charge; Ohm's law in vector form is j = σE.
At constant temperature and physical conditions, the current through a conductor is proportional to the potential difference across it: V = IR, R being independent of V and I.
The ratio V/I for a conductor, R = ρl/A. Unit ohm (Ω) = V A<sup>−1</sup>. Depends on material, dimensions and temperature.
The resistance of a unit cube of a material, ρ = RA/l, unit Ω m. Depends only on the material and its temperature, not on dimensions; ρ = m/(ne<sup>2</sup>τ).
Reciprocal of resistivity, σ = 1/ρ = ne<sup>2</sup>τ/m = neμ, unit S m<sup>−1</sup>. Conductance G = 1/R has unit siemens (S).
The average velocity with which free electrons move in a conductor under an applied field, superposed on their random thermal motion: v<sub>d</sub> = eEτ/m, of order mm s<sup>−1</sup>, opposite to E.
The average time between two successive collisions of a free electron with the ions of the lattice, τ ≈ 10<sup>−14</sup> s in metals. It decreases with temperature.
Magnitude of drift velocity per unit electric field, μ = |v<sub>d</sub>|/E = eτ/m. SI unit m<sup>2</sup> V<sup>−1</sup> s<sup>−1</sup>; σ = neμ.
Ohmic conductors have a linear V–I graph through the origin (metals). Non-ohmic devices such as a p–n diode or GaAs have non-linear, asymmetric or non-unique V–I graphs.

α in ρ<sub>T</sub> = ρ<sub>0</sub>[1 + α(T − T<sub>0</sub>)], the fractional change in resistivity per degree. Positive for metals, nearly zero for manganin and constantan, negative for semiconductors.
Rate at which energy is dissipated as heat in a conductor, P = VI = I<sup>2</sup>R = V<sup>2</sup>/R, unit watt.

The potential difference between the terminals of a cell when no current is drawn; equivalently the work done per unit charge by the cell in moving positive charge from its negative to its positive terminal. Unit volt.
The resistance offered by the electrolyte of a cell to the flow of current through it, r. Terminal voltage V = ε − Ir.
Potential difference across the terminals of a cell while it delivers current: V = ε − Ir (discharging) or V = ε + Ir (charging).
At any junction the sum of currents entering equals the sum leaving; a consequence of conservation of charge in steady flow.
The algebraic sum of potential changes around any closed loop is zero; a consequence of the potential being single-valued (conservation of energy).

Four resistors in a quadrilateral with a cell across one diagonal and a galvanometer across the other. Balanced (I<sub>g</sub> = 0) when R<sub>2</sub>/R<sub>1</sub> = R<sub>4</sub>/R<sub>3</sub>; a null method for measuring resistance.

ncert_questions.q: (a) Estimate the average drift speed of conduction electrons in a copper wire of cross-sectional area 1.0 × 10<sup>−7</sup> m<sup>2</sup> carrying a current of 1.5 A. Take the density of conduction electrons as 8.5 × 10<sup>28</sup> m<sup>−3</sup>. (b) Compare it with the thermal speed of electrons at room temperature and with the speed at which the electric field is set up along the wire.
ncert_questions.a:
(a) I = neAvd, so vd = I/(neA) = 1.5/(8.5 × 1028 × 1.6 × 10−19 × 1.0 × 10−7) = 1.5/(1.36 × 103) = 1.1 × 10−3 m s−1, about 1 mm per second.

(b) The thermal speed of an electron at 300 K is about √(kBT/m) ~ 105 m s−1, so the drift speed is smaller by a factor of about 10−8. The electric field is established along the wire at close to the speed of light, 3 × 108 m s−1, which is about 1011 times the drift speed. That is why the current starts everywhere in the circuit almost at once although each electron drifts very slowly.

ncert_questions.q: An electric toaster uses nichrome for its heating element. When a negligible current passes through it, its resistance at room temperature (27.0 °C) is 75.3 Ω. When the toaster is connected to a 230 V supply the current settles, after a few seconds, to a steady value of 2.68 A. What is the steady temperature of the nichrome element? The temperature coefficient of resistance of nichrome averaged over the temperature range involved is 1.70 × 10<sup>−4</sup> °C<sup>−1</sup>.
ncert_questions.a:
Resistance at the steady temperature: R2 = V/I = 230/2.68 = 85.8 Ω.

Using R2 = R1[1 + α(T2 − T1)]: T2 − T1 = (R2 − R1)/(R1α) = (85.8 − 75.3)/(75.3 × 1.70 × 10−4) = 10.5/(1.28 × 10−2) ≈ 820 °C.

Steady temperature T2 = 27 + 820 = 847 °C (approximately).

ncert_questions.q: The resistance of the platinum wire of a platinum resistance thermometer at the ice point is 5 Ω and at steam point is 5.23 Ω. When the thermometer is inserted in a hot bath, the resistance of the platinum wire is 5.795 Ω. Calculate the temperature of the bath.
ncert_questions.a:
Taking R0 = 5 Ω at 0 °C and R100 = 5.23 Ω at 100 °C, the resistance varies linearly: Rt = R0(1 + αt).

t = (Rt − R0)/(R100 − R0) × 100 = (5.795 − 5)/(5.23 − 5) × 100 = (0.795/0.23) × 100 = 345.65 °C.

The bath is at about 345.7 °C.

ncert_questions.q: A battery of 10 V and negligible internal resistance is connected across the diagonally opposite corners of a cubical network consisting of 12 resistors each of resistance 1 Ω. Determine the equivalent resistance of the network and the current along each edge of the cube.
ncert_questions.a:
Let the current entering corner A be 3I. By the symmetry of the cube the three edges at A are equivalent, so each carries I. At the next corners each current I splits equally into two: the six middle edges carry I/2 each. By the same symmetry the three edges meeting at the opposite corner A' carry I each, adding up to 3I.

Apply the loop rule along any path from A to A' through the battery, taking each edge as R: −IR − (I/2)R − IR + ε = 0, so ε = (5/2)IR.

Equivalent resistance Req = ε/(3I) = (5/2)IR/(3I) = 5R/6 = 5/6 Ω for R = 1 Ω.

Total current 3I = ε/Req = 10/(5/6) = 12 A, so I = 4 A: the edges at the two battery corners carry 4 A each and the six middle edges carry 2 A each.

ncert_questions.q: The four arms of a Wheatstone bridge have resistances AB = 100 Ω, BC = 10 Ω, CD = 5 Ω and DA = 60 Ω. A galvanometer of 15 Ω resistance is connected across BD. Calculate the current through the galvanometer when a potential difference of 10 V is maintained across AC.
ncert_questions.a:
Let I1 be the current from A through the 100 Ω arm AB, continuing after the galvanometer junction at B through the 10 Ω arm BC as (I1 − Ig); let I2 be the current from A through the 60 Ω arm AD, continuing through the 5 Ω arm DC as (I2 + Ig); and let Ig be the galvanometer current from B to D.

Loop BADB: 100I1 + 15Ig − 60I2 = 0, i.e. 20I1 + 3Ig − 12I2 = 0 … (1)

Loop BCDB: 10(I1 − Ig) − 15Ig − 5(I2 + Ig) = 0, i.e. 2I1 − 6Ig − I2 = 0 … (2)

Loop ADCA (through the source): 60I2 + 5(I2 + Ig) = 10, i.e. 13I2 + Ig = 2 … (3)

Multiplying (2) by 10: 20I1 − 60Ig − 10I2 = 0 … (4). Subtracting (1) from (4): −63Ig + 2I2 = 0, so I2 = 31.5Ig.

Substituting in (3): 13(31.5Ig) + Ig = 2 → 410.5Ig = 2 → Ig = 4.87 × 10−3 A = 4.87 mA.

The bridge is unbalanced, since AB/BC = 10 is not equal to DA/DC = 12, so the simple balance condition does not apply and the full set of Kirchhoff loop equations is needed.

ncert_questions.q: The storage battery of a car has an emf of 12 V. If the internal resistance of the battery is 0.4 Ω, what is the maximum current that can be drawn from the battery?
ncert_questions.a: The current is maximum when the external resistance is zero: Imax = ε/r = 12/0.4 = 30 A.

ncert_questions.q: A battery of emf 10 V and internal resistance 3 Ω is connected to a resistor. If the current in the circuit is 0.5 A, what is the resistance of the resistor? What is the terminal voltage of the battery when the circuit is closed?
ncert_questions.a:
I = ε/(R + r) gives R + r = 10/0.5 = 20 Ω, so R = 20 − 3 = 17 Ω.

Terminal voltage V = IR = 0.5 × 17 = 8.5 V (check: ε − Ir = 10 − 0.5 × 3 = 8.5 V).

ncert_questions.q: At room temperature (27.0 °C) the resistance of a heating element is 100 Ω. What is the temperature of the element if the resistance is found to be 117 Ω, given that the temperature coefficient of the material of the resistor is 1.70 × 10<sup>−4</sup> °C<sup>−1</sup>?

A negligibly small current is passed through a wire of length 15 m and uniform cross-section 6.0 × 10<sup>−7</sup> m<sup>2</sup>, and its resistance is measured to be 5.0 Ω. What is the resistivity of the material at the temperature of the experiment?
A silver wire has a resistance of 2.1 Ω at 27.5 °C and a resistance of 2.7 Ω at 100 °C. Determine the temperature coefficient of resistivity of silver.

A heating element using nichrome connected to a 230 V supply draws an initial current of 3.2 A which settles after a few seconds to a steady value of 2.8 A. What is the steady temperature of the heating element if the room temperature is 27.0 °C? Temperature coefficient of resistance of nichrome averaged over the temperature range involved is 1.70 × 10<sup>−4</sup> °C<sup>−1</sup>.
ncert_questions.a:
Initial (room temperature) resistance R1 = 230/3.2 = 71.9 Ω. Steady resistance R2 = 230/2.8 = 82.1 Ω.

T2 − T1 = (R2 − R1)/(R1α) = (82.1 − 71.9)/(71.9 × 1.70 × 10−4) = 10.3/(1.22 × 10−2) ≈ 840 °C.

Steady temperature T2 = 27 + 840 = 867 °C.

ncert_questions.q: Determine the current in each branch of the network shown in the figure: a 10 V battery with a 10 Ω resistor in series is connected between A and C of a network in which AB = 10 Ω, BC = 5 Ω, AD = 5 Ω, DC = 10 Ω and BD = 5 Ω.
ncert_questions.a:
Let the total current be I, splitting at A into I1 along AB and I − I1 along AD; let I2 flow from D to B through the 5 Ω between them. Then BC carries I1 + I2 and DC carries I − I1 − I2.

Loop ABDA: −10I1 + 5I2 + 5(I − I1) = 0 → 3I1 − I2 = I.

Loop BCDB: −5(I1 + I2) + 10(I − I1 − I2) − 5I2 = 0 → 3I1 + 4I2 = 2I.

Subtracting: 5I2 = I, so I2 = I/5 and I1 = 2I/5.

Outer loop through the battery (A → D → C → battery): 10 − 10I − 5(I − I1) − 10(I − I1 − I2) = 0 → 10 = 10I + 3I + 4I = 17I, so I = 10/17 A.

Currents: AB = 2I/5 = 4/17 A; AD = 3I/5 = 6/17 A; DB = 2/17 A (from D to B); BC = 4/17 + 2/17 = 6/17 A; DC = 6/17 − 2/17 = 4/17 A; total current 10/17 A. Check: VA − VC = 10 × 4/17 + 5 × 6/17 = 70/17 V by either path.

ncert_questions.q: A storage battery of emf 8.0 V and internal resistance 0.5 Ω is being charged by a 120 V dc supply using a series resistor of 15.5 Ω. What is the terminal voltage of the battery during charging? What is the purpose of having a series resistor in the charging circuit?
ncert_questions.a:
Charging current I = (120 − 8)/(15.5 + 0.5) = 112/16 = 7 A.

During charging the terminal voltage exceeds the emf: V = ε + Ir = 8 + 7 × 0.5 = 11.5 V.

The series resistor limits the charging current to a safe value; without it the current would be (120 − 8)/0.5 = 224 A, which would damage the battery.

pyq.q: A wire of resistance R is stretched uniformly so that its length becomes double. Its new resistance is
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: Volume is constant, so doubling the length halves the area. R' = ρ(2l)/(A/2) = 4ρl/A = 4R.

pyq.q: Two bulbs rated 100 W, 220 V and 60 W, 220 V are connected in series across a 220 V supply. Then
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: R = V<sup>2</sup>/P, so the 60 W bulb has the larger resistance (807 Ω against 484 Ω). In series the current is the same and P = I<sup>2</sup>R, so the 60 W bulb dissipates more power and glows brighter.

pyq.q: A potential difference V is applied across a conductor of length l. If the length is doubled keeping V the same, the drift velocity of the electrons
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: v<sub>d</sub> = eEτ/m with E = V/l. Doubling l at the same V halves E, so the drift velocity is halved.

pyq.q: The resistivity of a semiconductor decreases as its temperature rises because
options: the number density of charge carriers increases
the mass of the carriers decreases
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: ρ = m/(ne<sup>2</sup>τ). In a semiconductor, heating frees many more carriers, so n rises much faster than τ falls and ρ decreases.

pyq.q: A cell of emf 2 V and internal resistance 1 Ω is connected to an external resistance of 4 Ω. The terminal voltage of the cell is
pyq.answer: b

pyq.q: In a Wheatstone bridge, the arms AB, BC and AD have resistances 2 Ω, 4 Ω and 6 Ω respectively. The bridge is balanced when the resistance in arm DC is
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: Balance: AB/BC = AD/DC, so 2/4 = 6/S, giving S = 12 Ω.

pyq.q: The V–I graphs of a metallic wire at two temperatures T<sub>1</sub> and T<sub>2</sub> are straight lines through the origin, V being plotted on the vertical axis. The line for T<sub>2</sub> makes a larger angle with the current axis than the line for T<sub>1</sub>. Then
options: nothing can be said about the temperatures
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: With V on the vertical axis the slope is R. The steeper line has the larger resistance, and the resistance of a metal increases with temperature, so T<sub>2</sub> > T<sub>1</sub>.

pyq.q: The SI unit of mobility of a charge carrier is
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: μ = v<sub>d</sub>/E has unit (m s<sup>−1</sup>)/(V m<sup>−1</sup>) = m<sup>2</sup> V<sup>−1</sup> s<sup>−1</sup>.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): When a 60 W bulb and a 100 W bulb, both rated 220 V, are connected in series across 220 V, the 60 W bulb glows brighter. Reason (R): In a series circuit the same current flows through both bulbs, so the bulb with the larger resistance dissipates more power.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: a
pyq.solution: The 60 W bulb has the larger resistance (R = V<sup>2</sup>/P), and with a common current P = I<sup>2</sup>R is larger for it. R correctly explains A.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): Alloys such as manganin and constantan are used to make standard resistances. Reason (R): These alloys have a high resistivity.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: Both statements are true, but the reason these alloys are chosen for standard resistances is their very small temperature coefficient of resistivity, so their resistance does not change with temperature. High resistivity is a convenience, not the deciding property.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): The resistivity of a semiconductor decreases with increase in temperature. Reason (R): The relaxation time of charge carriers in a semiconductor increases with temperature.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: A is true. R is false: relaxation time decreases with temperature in every material. The resistivity falls because the number density n of carriers rises steeply.

pyq.q: Define the term 'mobility' of charge carriers in a conductor. Write its SI unit and the relation between mobility and conductivity.
pyq.answer:
Mobility is the magnitude of the drift velocity acquired by a charge carrier per unit electric field: μ = |vd|/E = eτ/m.

SI unit: m2 V−1 s−1. Relation with conductivity: σ = neμ, where n is the number density of carriers and e the charge of each.

pyq.q: Two wires A and B of the same material and the same length have radii in the ratio 1 : 2. Find the ratio of the drift velocities of electrons in them when they are connected (i) in series, (ii) in parallel across a source.
pyq.answer:
(i) In series the current is the same, and I = neAvd, so vd ∝ 1/A ∝ 1/r2. Hence vA : vB = rB2 : rA2 = 4 : 1.

(ii) In parallel the potential difference is the same and the lengths are equal, so the field E = V/l is the same in both. vd = eEτ/m depends only on E for the same material, so vA : vB = 1 : 1.

pyq.q: Plot a graph showing the variation of terminal voltage V of a cell with the current I drawn from it. How can the emf and the internal resistance of the cell be obtained from this graph?
pyq.answer:
V = ε − Ir, so the graph of V against I is a straight line with negative slope: it starts at V = ε on the V-axis (I = 0) and falls to V = 0 at I = ε/r on the I-axis.

The intercept on the V-axis gives the emf ε. The magnitude of the slope of the line gives the internal resistance r (r = −ΔV/ΔI); equivalently r = ε/I0, where I0 is the intercept on the current axis.

pyq.q: Why is nichrome used for the heating element of an electric heater, and manganin for making standard resistance coils?
pyq.answer:
Nichrome has a high resistivity (about 60 times that of copper), a high melting point and does not oxidise easily even when red hot. A short wire therefore produces a large amount of heat (H = I2Rt) and survives at high temperature.

Manganin has a very small temperature coefficient of resistivity together with a fairly high resistivity, so the resistance of a manganin coil stays practically constant as it warms up in use, which is what a standard resistance needs.

pyq.q: A cell of emf 6 V and internal resistance 0.5 Ω is connected to an external resistor of 5.5 Ω. Calculate the current in the circuit and the terminal voltage of the cell.
Define drift velocity. On the basis of the drift of free electrons, derive the expression for the current in a conductor, I = neAv<sub>d</sub>, and hence obtain Ohm's law.
pyq.answer:
Drift velocity is the average velocity with which free electrons move in a conductor under an applied electric field, superposed on their random thermal motion. With acceleration eE/m for a mean time τ between collisions, vd = eEτ/m (magnitude), directed opposite to E.

Current. Consider a conductor of cross-section A with n free electrons per unit volume. In time Δt every electron within a length vdΔt of a chosen cross-section crosses it. Number crossing = n(AvdΔt); charge crossing = neAvdΔt. Hence I = charge/time = neAvd.

Ohm's law. Substituting vd = eEτ/m with E = V/l: I = neA(eVτ)/(ml) = (ne2τA/(ml))V. So V = I × [ml/(ne2τA)] = IR, with R = ρl/A and ρ = m/(ne2τ). Since n and τ are independent of V, R is constant, which is Ohm's law.

pyq.q: Two cells of emfs ε<sub>1</sub> and ε<sub>2</sub> and internal resistances r<sub>1</sub> and r<sub>2</sub> are connected in parallel. Derive expressions for the emf and internal resistance of the equivalent cell.
pyq.answer:
Connect the positive terminals at B1 and the negative terminals at B2, and let the cells supply currents I1 and I2, so the current to the external circuit is I = I1 + I2. Both cells have the same terminal voltage V:

V = ε1 − I1r1 → I1 = (ε1 − V)/r1; V = ε2 − I2r2 → I2 = (ε2 − V)/r2.

Adding: I = (ε1/r1 + ε2/r2) − V(1/r1 + 1/r2), so

V = (ε1r2 + ε2r1)/(r1 + r2) − I r1r2/(r1 + r2).

Comparing with V = εeq − Ireq for a single equivalent cell: εeq = (ε1r2 + ε2r1)/(r1 + r2) and req = r1r2/(r1 + r2), i.e. 1/req = 1/r1 + 1/r2.

pyq.q: Using Kirchhoff's rules, find the current in each branch of the circuit in which a 12 V cell of internal resistance 2 Ω and a 6 V cell of internal resistance 1 Ω are connected in parallel (positive terminals together) across a 4 Ω resistor.
pyq.answer:
Let I1 be the current from the 12 V cell and I2 from the 6 V cell, both towards the common positive node; by the junction rule the 4 Ω resistor carries I1 + I2.

Loop through the 12 V cell and the 4 Ω resistor: 12 − 2I1 − 4(I1 + I2) = 0 → 6I1 + 4I2 = 12 … (1)

Loop through the 6 V cell and the 4 Ω resistor: 6 − 1·I2 − 4(I1 + I2) = 0 → 4I1 + 5I2 = 6 … (2)

From (1) × 2 − (2) × 3: 12I1 + 8I2 − 12I1 − 15I2 = 24 − 18 → −7I2 = 6 → I2 = −6/7 A ≈ −0.86 A.

From (1): 6I1 = 12 + 24/7 = 108/7 → I1 = 18/7 A ≈ 2.57 A. Current in the 4 Ω resistor = I1 + I2 = 12/7 A ≈ 1.71 A.

The negative sign shows that 6/7 A flows into the 6 V cell through its positive terminal: it is being charged by the 12 V cell.

pyq.q: Draw a circuit diagram of a Wheatstone bridge and use Kirchhoff's rules to obtain the condition for its balance.
pyq.answer:
Figure: resistors R1 (AB), R2 (BC), R3 (AD), R4 (DC), a cell between A and C, a galvanometer G between B and D.

Let the current I from the cell divide at A into I1 through R1 and I2 through R3. At balance the galvanometer current Ig = 0, so by the junction rule I1 flows on through R2 and I2 through R4.

Loop ADBA: −I2R3 + I1R1 = 0 → I1R1 = I2R3 … (1)

Loop CBDC: I2R4 − I1R2 = 0 → I1R2 = I2R4 … (2)

Dividing (2) by (1): R2/R1 = R4/R3. This is the balance condition; it does not involve the galvanometer resistance or the cell, so an unknown R4 = R2R3/R1 can be found by a null method.

pyq.q: Two heating coils A and B, connected one at a time to the same supply, boil a given amount of water in 10 minutes and 15 minutes respectively. How long will the same water take to boil if the coils are connected (i) in series, (ii) in parallel across the same supply?
pyq.answer:
At fixed voltage the heat produced in time t is H = V2t/R, so for the same H the time is proportional to the resistance: t ∝ R. Thus RA ∝ 10 and RB ∝ 15.

(i) Series: R = RA + RB, so t = tA + tB = 10 + 15 = 25 min.

(ii) Parallel: 1/R = 1/RA + 1/RB, so 1/t = 1/10 + 1/15 = 5/30, giving t = tAtB/(tA + tB) = 150/25 = 6 min.

pyq.q: (a) Derive an expression for the drift velocity of free electrons in a conductor in terms of the relaxation time. Hence obtain the expression for the resistivity of the material, ρ = m/(ne<sup>2</sup>τ). (b) Using this expression, explain how the resistivity of (i) a metal and (ii) a semiconductor changes with temperature.
pyq.answer:
(a) Drift velocity. Each free electron (mass m, charge −e) in a field E has acceleration a = −eE/m. Between collisions it accelerates; at each collision with the lattice ions its velocity is reset to a random thermal value whose average over all electrons is zero. If τ is the average time between collisions (relaxation time), the average extra velocity acquired since the last collision is aτ. So the average velocity of the electrons is vd = −eEτ/m, the drift velocity, of constant magnitude eEτ/m and opposite to E.

Resistivity. With n electrons per unit volume, the charge crossing area A in time Δt is neAvdΔt, so I = neAvd and j = I/A = nevd = (ne2τ/m)E. Comparing with j = σE = E/ρ gives σ = ne2τ/m and ρ = m/(ne2τ).

(b) Temperature dependence. ρ depends on n and τ. (i) In a metal n is fixed, but with rising temperature the ions vibrate more and the electrons collide more often, so τ decreases and ρ increases: metals have a positive temperature coefficient, ρT = ρ0[1 + α(T − T0)]. (ii) In a semiconductor, heating releases many more charge carriers, so n increases rapidly with temperature; this outweighs the fall in τ, and ρ decreases with temperature: the temperature coefficient is negative.

pyq.q: (a) State Kirchhoff's rules for an electrical network and mention the conservation law on which each is based. (b) Use them to derive the balance condition of a Wheatstone bridge. (c) In a balanced Wheatstone bridge the cell and the galvanometer are interchanged. Will the bridge remain balanced? Justify.
pyq.answer:
(a) Junction rule: at any junction the sum of currents entering equals the sum of currents leaving; it is based on conservation of charge (no accumulation of charge at a junction in a steady current). Loop rule: the algebraic sum of the changes in potential around any closed loop is zero; it is based on the potential being single-valued, i.e. on conservation of energy.

(b) Let R1, R2, R3, R4 be in arms AB, BC, AD, DC, the cell across AC and the galvanometer across BD. The current divides at A into I1 (through R1) and I2 (through R3). At balance Ig = 0, so I1 continues through R2 and I2 through R4. Loop ADBA: I1R1 − I2R3 = 0. Loop CBDC: I2R4 − I1R2 = 0. Dividing, R2/R1 = R4/R3, which is the balance condition.

(c) Yes. The balance condition R2/R1 = R4/R3 can be rewritten as R3/R1 = R4/R2, which is exactly the balance condition with the cell across BD and the galvanometer across AC. Since the condition involves neither the cell nor the galvanometer, interchanging them leaves the bridge balanced.

pyq.q: (a) Define emf and internal resistance of a cell. Obtain the relation between the terminal voltage, emf and internal resistance of a cell when it is connected to an external resistance R, and draw the graphs of terminal voltage against (i) R and (ii) the current I. (b) A cell supplies a current of 0.5 A when connected to a 2 Ω resistor and 0.4 A when connected to a 2.6 Ω resistor. Find its emf and internal resistance.
pyq.answer:
(a) The emf ε of a cell is the potential difference between its terminals when no current is drawn from it, i.e. the work done per unit charge by the cell in moving positive charge from its negative to its positive terminal. The internal resistance r is the resistance offered by the electrolyte of the cell to the current through it.

With external resistance R, the current is I = ε/(R + r). The terminal voltage is the potential difference across R: V = IR = εR/(R + r), and rearranging, V = ε − Ir. The drop Ir occurs inside the cell, so V < ε whenever current flows.

Graphs: (i) V against R rises from zero at R = 0 and approaches ε asymptotically for large R. (ii) V against I is a straight line with intercept ε on the V-axis and slope −r, meeting the I-axis at I = ε/r.

(b) ε = I1(R1 + r) = I2(R2 + r): 0.5(2 + r) = 0.4(2.6 + r) → 1.0 + 0.5r = 1.04 + 0.4r → 0.1r = 0.04 → r = 0.4 Ω.

ε = 0.5 × (2 + 0.4) = 1.2 V (check: 0.4 × (2.6 + 0.4) = 1.2 V).

pyq.q:
The resistivity of a material is given by ρ = m/(ne2τ), where n is the number density of free electrons and τ the relaxation time. In metals n is practically constant, while τ decreases as the temperature rises because the lattice ions vibrate more vigorously. In semiconductors the number of free carriers rises rapidly with temperature. Over a limited range, ρT = ρ0[1 + α(T − T0)], where α is the temperature coefficient of resistivity. Alloys such as manganin and nichrome have high resistivity and very small α.
(i) Why does the resistivity of a metal increase with temperature?
(ii) What is the sign of α for a semiconductor, and why?
(iii) The resistance of a copper coil is 100 Ω at 27 °C. Taking α = 4 × 10−3 °C−1, find its resistance at 127 °C.
(iv) Which of manganin and nichrome would you choose for a resistance box, and why?
pyq.answer:
(i) n is constant in a metal but τ decreases with temperature because collisions with the vibrating ions become more frequent; since ρ ∝ 1/τ, ρ rises.

(ii) Negative. Heating a semiconductor frees many more charge carriers, so n increases much faster than τ falls, and ρ decreases with temperature.

(iii) RT = R0[1 + α(T − T0)] = 100[1 + 4 × 10−3 × (127 − 27)] = 100 × (1 + 0.4) = 140 Ω.

(iv) Manganin, because its temperature coefficient is almost zero, so the resistance of the coils stays fixed as they warm up in use; nichrome is chosen for heating elements instead, where high resistivity and heat tolerance matter.

pyq.q:
A cell converts chemical energy into electrical energy. Its emf ε is the potential difference between its terminals in an open circuit, and its electrolyte offers an internal resistance r. When a resistance R is connected across it, a current I = ε/(R + r) flows and the terminal voltage falls to V = ε − Ir. During charging the current is driven into the cell and the terminal voltage becomes ε + Ir. Cells can be combined in series to raise the emf or in parallel to lower the effective internal resistance.
(i) Why is the terminal voltage of a cell less than its emf when it supplies current?
(ii) A cell of emf 1.5 V and internal resistance 0.5 Ω is connected to a 2.5 Ω resistor. Find the terminal voltage.
(iii) Under what condition is the terminal voltage equal to the emf?
(iv) Two identical cells each of emf ε and internal resistance r are connected in parallel. Write the emf and internal resistance of the combination.
pyq.answer:
(i) Part of the emf is used up in driving the current through the internal resistance of the cell: the drop Ir occurs inside the cell, so the potential difference available at the terminals is V = ε − Ir < ε.

(ii) I = ε/(R + r) = 1.5/(2.5 + 0.5) = 0.5 A; V = IR = 0.5 × 2.5 = 1.25 V (or ε − Ir = 1.5 − 0.25 = 1.25 V).

(iii) When no current is drawn (open circuit, I = 0), or if the internal resistance is negligible (r = 0).

(iv) εeq = ε (from (εr + εr)/(r + r)), and req = r/2.

common_mistakes: Writing that drift velocity is proportional to the current. It is proportional to the electric field, v<sub>d</sub> = eEτ/m; in parallel wires of equal length the drift velocity is the same however thick the wires are, and in series wires it varies as 1/A.

Using the rated power of a bulb directly when bulbs are in series. First convert each rating to a resistance with R = V<sup>2</sup>/P, then compare I<sup>2</sup>R with the common current; the lower-wattage bulb glows brighter.
Stating that emf is a force or that it is measured in newtons. Emf is work per unit charge, measured in volts, and it is the terminal potential difference only when no current flows.

Explaining the temperature dependence of resistivity without ρ = m/(ne<sup>2</sup>τ). The marking scheme wants the sentence: in metals τ decreases so ρ rises; in semiconductors n increases so ρ falls.

Changing the sign convention halfway through a Kirchhoff problem, or taking a loop that is the sum of two loops already used. Fix the traversal direction, write +ε from negative to positive terminal and −IR along the current, and use as many independent loops as unknowns.

Forgetting that a stretched wire keeps its volume, so doubling the length quadruples the resistance, and forgetting that cutting a wire into n parts and putting them in parallel gives R/n<sup>2</sup>.

Writing the Wheatstone balance condition without the derivation when the question asks 'using Kirchhoff's rules', or forgetting to state I<sub>g</sub> = 0 and the two loop equations before dividing them.

Giving the parallel-cells formula with the wrong pairing, ε<sub>1</sub>r<sub>1</sub> + ε<sub>2</sub>r<sub>2</sub>. The correct numerator is ε<sub>1</sub>r<sub>2</sub> + ε<sub>2</sub>r<sub>1</sub>; check that ε<sub>eq</sub> lies between the two emfs.
strategy:
Give this chapter two focused sessions. In the first, master the microscopic model: write out the drift-velocity derivation from a = eE/m to ρ = m/(ne2τ) three times without looking, adding the definition of mobility and the one-line explanation of the temperature dependence of metals and semiconductors. Then learn the three V–I graphs of section 3.6 and the three ρ–T graphs of section 3.8, because a 2-mark question on these needs a correct sketch, not prose.

In the second session work the circuit side. Derive V = ε − Ir and the two graphs of terminal voltage, then the parallel-cells formula, then the Wheatstone balance from Kirchhoff's rules, each with a labelled figure. After that solve at least six Kirchhoff problems with two cells in different branches, including NCERT Exercise 3.7, and check every answer by computing the potential difference between two nodes along two different paths. Practise the temperature numericals (Examples 3.3, 3.4, Exercises 3.3, 3.5, 3.6) until finding R from V/I and then T from α is automatic.

Memorise a short list: units of current density, mobility, conductivity and resistivity; the typical values (vd ~ mm s−1, τ ~ 10−14 s, n ~ 1029 m−3); which alloy goes where and why; and the formula for a stretched wire. In the paper, budget about 2 minutes per mark, draw the circuit before writing any equation, and always carry units into the final line.
